answer:
FULL ANALYSIS EXECUTED — SYNTHESIS-READY RESULTS

NATURAL-LANGUAGE HYPOTHESIS (final answer draft):
"Across the NLSY79 cohort (N = 12,013; 289 individuals jailed at some point during 1985–1994), individuals with a criminal record had significantly lower wealth than those without a record in ALL THREE years examined — 1985, 1990, and 1996 (all p < 0.001 on Welch t-tests and Mann–Whitney U tests, and all p < 0.05 in race/sex-adjusted robust regressions). The wealth gap widened over time: jailed individuals averaged ~$7,929 vs ~$25,086 in 1985 (mean difference ≈ −$17,157), ~$16,350 vs ~$73,948 in 1990 (≈ −$57,598), and ~$20,383 vs ~$105,447 in 1996 (≈ −$85,064), with medians of $720 vs $3,600 (1985), $0 vs $10,500 (1990), and $0 vs $8,500 (1996). Importantly, the timing frame changes the interpretation: because ever_jailed covers only 1985–1994, the significant 1985 gap is best read as a PRE-EXISTING (pre-incarceration/selection) difference rather than an effect of incarceration, whereas the significant 1990 and 1996 gaps — especially the much larger 1996 gap — are consistent with wealth divergence during and after the incarceration window. The data show association, not causation."

WHICH YEARS ARE "SIGNIFICANTLY LOWER": ALL THREE (1985, 1990, 1996), with NO test disagreement anywhere — Welch t-test, one-sided Mann–Whitney (H1: jailed < not-jailed), winsorized t-test, HC3-adjusted OLS, and median (quantile) regression all reject at α = 0.05 in every year.

KEY NUMBERS (unadjusted, jailed n=289 vs not-jailed n=11,724):
- 1985: Welch t = −9.78, p = 6.3e−21; MWU p(one-sided less) = 8.0e−11 (two-sided 1.6e−10); mean diff −17,157
- 1990: Welch t = −9.57, p = 1.6e−19; MWU p(less) = 3.9e−35 (two-sided 7.8e−35); mean diff −57,598
- 1996: Welch t = −9.72, p = 7.3e−20; MWU p(less) = 4.6e−26 (two-sided 9.3e−26); mean diff −85,064

ADJUSTED (race + sex, HC3-robust OLS), ever_jailed coefficient:
- 1985: −9,441 (95% CI [−13,043, −5,839]), p = 2.8e−07
- 1990: −35,394 (95% CI [−47,796, −22,992]), p = 2.2e−08
- 1996: −60,911 (95% CI [−78,761, −43,061]), p = 2.3e−11
Median (quantile) regression coefficients (adjusted): −1,100 (p=0.021), −3,800 (p=0.016), −6,000 (p=0.0003) — smaller because medians sit near zero for the jailed group, but all still significant at 0.05.
Sensitivity: winsorized (1%/99%) Welch t-tests: p = 9.3e−16 / 8.8e−27 / 7.7e−35 for 1985/1990/1996 — conclusions robust to outliers.

METHODOLOGY NOTES HONORING THE APPROVED PLAN:
- Negatives retained as-is (net worth interpretation); original data values were never modified — 'hipanic' handled only via label mapping in the model formula, and no altered dataset was saved (artifacts are the script plus two output CSVs of results).
- Female×jailed cell (n=37; race×sex cells as small as n=9) flagged UNDERPOWERED: stratified medians for jailed individuals are $0 in every race×sex cell in 1990/1996, directionally consistent with the aggregate gap, but no subgroup-level significance claims are made.
- R² of adjusted models is small (0.009–0.019): ever_jailed, race and sex explain little wealth variance overall — the gap is significant but wealth is dominated by other (unobserved) factors.

TIMING NUANCE (explicitly in the hypothesis wording, per your instruction): "found to have significantly lower wealth" is reported as association in all three years, with 1985 interpreted as a pre-existing gap (pre-incarceration), 1990 as mixed during-window, and 1996 as post-incarceration. No causal claim.

LIMITATIONS / UNCERTAINTIES:
1. Units/scale of composite wealth undocumented (assumed USD); exact composition of the "five wealth variables" unknown.
2. ever_jailed misses arrests without jail; "criminal record" is operationalized narrowly.
3. No survey weights or attrition correction available in the processed file.
4. Heavy right skew (6.5–16.8) and ~3–5% zeros/negatives — hence the dual-test approach; MWU and t-test agree everywhere, so no interpretive conflict to report.
5. Adjusted models control only for race and sex; residual confounding (education, family background, prior wealth) is unaddressed, reinforcing the non-causal framing.

Artifacts: analysis/wealth_vs_jailed.py (executed script), analysis/group_descriptives.csv, analysis/unadjusted_tests.csv. Full console output above includes all test statistics, p-values, CIs, stratum counts, and stratified medians.

payload.hypothesis: Individuals with a criminal record (jailed 1985-1994) had significantly lower wealth than those without a record in all three years — 1985, 1990, and 1996 (all unadjusted and adjusted p<0.05). The gap widened over time (mean difference ~-$17k in 1985, ~-$58k in 1990, ~-$85k in 1996; jailed-group medians $720/$0/$0 vs $3,600/$10,500/$8,500). Because ever_jailed covers only 1985-1994, the significant 1985 gap reflects pre-existing (pre-incarceration) differences, while 1990 and 1996 — especially the larger 1996 gap — are consistent with wealth divergence during and after incarceration. This is an association, not a causal claim.
payload.workflow: Loaded data (12,013 rows, zero missing); verified negatives in all wealth years (net worth interpretation). Per-year two-group comparisons (ever_jailed 1 vs 0, n=289 vs 11,724): Welch t-tests, one/two-sided Mann-Whitney U, winsorized (1%/99%) t-test sensitivity; adjusted HC3-robust OLS and median (quantile) regression with race and sex covariates ('hipanic' mapped for modeling only, original values untouched); stratified race×sex descriptives with underpowered-cell flags. Verdict at alpha=0.05: all three years significant on every test; timing interpretation: 1985 pre-incarceration selection, 1990 during-window, 1996 post-incarceration.
